paras: The anonymous letters to Black tenants near Clarendon, Arkansas, were warnings sent in late June 1903 to the Black residents of the Fowler-Coburn neighborhood, a plantation district outside the town, telling them that "the quickest way out of the country was the best." A general departure of the Black farm workers seemed imminent until white landowners who lived in Clarendon visited the district on June 30 and promised protection, after which the tenants agreed to stay. A Clarendon dispatch in the Newport Daily Independent presented the letters as the "financial side" of troubles in the neighborhood that had included a killing and a lynching.

According to the Clarendon correspondent, the troubles in the Fowler-Coburn neighborhood began with "the killing of Fowler" and culminated in "the lynching of Harris, the assailant of Coburn." Most of the plantations in the district belonged to men who lived in Clarendon, and they were worked by Black laborers.

After the lynching, the Black residents of the neighborhood received anonymous letters urging them to leave the country, and the dispatch described a "general exodus" as imminent. Hearing that they might lose their labor through "the intimidation of unknown parties," a number of the landowners went out to the district on the afternoon of June 30 to persuade the tenants to remain. On a promise of protection from the landlords and "the best citizens of that section," the tenants consented to stay.

The writers of the letters were not identified; the paper reported only that they were "generally believed" to be "irresponsible white renters" who hoped to cheapen rents by creating a scarcity of labor. No arrests or official action appear in the coverage, and no later report shows whether any of the tenants left.

The episode is known from a single Clarendon dispatch dated July 1, printed in the Newport Daily Independent on July 2 under the headline "Frightened Negroes Threaten Exodus" and repeated in the Newport Weekly Independent the next day. The item told the story largely from the landowners' side, stressing the "considerable loss" the tenants' departure would have caused and calling the residents "darkies" and "frightened blacks." It closed by saying "the better class of white farmers" wanted order restored and regretted that "a few reckless ones" had given the community a reputation for lawlessness.
No coverage of the letters in the Black press was found.

reader.title: Anonymous letters to Black tenants near Clarendon, Arkansas
bases: Unknown parties sent anonymous letters telling the Black residents of a plantation district to leave the country; no violence against them is reported (A3).
The only account is the Clarendon dispatch in the Newport Daily Independent (A3); the Newport Weekly Independent item (A5) is the same text from the same publisher, not an independent report.

accounts.label: Clarendon correspondent
accounts.gist: Anonymous letters frightened the Black residents into preparing to leave; their landlords, worried about losing their labor, promised protection and the tenants consented to stay. The letters were believed to come from white renters seeking cheaper rents.

framing.detail: The Newport Daily Independent headlined it "Frightened Negroes Threaten Exodus," called the residents "darkies" and "frightened blacks," stressed the landowners' potential loss, and blamed "a few reckless" white renters for the district's reputation for lawlessness.
The Newport Weekly Independent ran the same item a day later.

set_aside: Clarendon, May 20: Riley Park, Black, shot J. O. Fowler ten miles east of Clarendon after a stock dispute and surrendered to Sheriff Milwee; the earlier episode the July dispatch names as the start of the neighborhood's troubles.
Clarendon, June 25: lynching of Jack Harris, accused assailant of John Coburn, by a mob of about fifty; says Black residents of the Coburn neighborhood had grown 'insolent'; a separate episode.
Report of the Harris lynching at Clarendon; seen in excerpt by research, not opened.
